summary: Defines a canonical address format for LISP control messages and for lookup keys in the LISP mapping database, so many kinds of addresses can be carried in one encoding. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: LCAF gives LISP control messages one format for carrying many kinds of addresses and related data. A type field tells the receiver how to read each value, and the RFC cautions that these experimental formats are incomplete.

questions: how does lisp encode instance id
subtitle: A common address envelope for carrying many kinds of values in LISP messages.

tldr.problem: LISP control messages and mapping lookups need to carry more than IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, including values such as instance identifiers, multicast data, and location information.
tldr.mechanism: LCAF assigns a dedicated Address Family Identifier and a type-and-length header so a receiver can interpret the payload that follows.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines approved and unapproved experimental encodings for cautious use in self-contained environments. It is Experimental and has been updated by RFC 9306 and RFC 10040.

today: RFC 8060 is an Experimental specification updated by RFC 9306 and RFC 10040. Its text describes the work as incomplete and the encodings as intended for cautious use in self-contained environments.

sections.title: Why LISP Uses LCAF
sections.content:
LISP uses Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) for hosts and Routing Locators (RLOCs) for tunnel routers. Its control messages encode addresses using an Address Family Identifier (AFI), length, and value. This document defines the LISP Canonical Address Format (LCAF) for LISP-specific encodings.

The RFC says its experimental types support experimentation and cautious use in self-contained environments. Specific uses are described in separate use-case documents, and the specification is explicitly incomplete.
sections.plainLanguage: LISP needs to carry values that ordinary IP address formats do not describe. LCAF adds a common wrapper that identifies how to interpret each value.

sections.title: The LCAF Header
sections.content:
The LCAF AFI is 16387 (0x4003). After that AFI, the format has a reserved byte, flags byte, type byte, another reserved byte, and a 16-bit length. The type identifies the payload format; the length counts the bytes after the length field.

Reserved fields and flags are sent as zero and ignored on receipt. Including the AFI, the minimum encoded address is 8 bytes; without the AFI, it is 6 bytes. The RFC also specifies sorting rules so locator sets have a consistent order.
sections.plainLanguage: The header identifies an LCAF value, names its type, and gives the payload length. A receiver uses the type to decide how to read what follows.

sections.title: Approved Address Encodings
sections.content:
The approved types include an AFI List, Instance ID, AS Number, Geo-Coordinates, NAT-Traversal, Multicast Info, Explicit Locator Path, Security Key, Source/Dest Key, and Replication List Entry. The AFI List can carry multiple encoded values, including IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, MAC addresses, ASCII names, or a nested LCAF value.

Other types add data for specific mapping uses. For example, Instance ID distinguishes overlapping address spaces, Geo-Coordinates attaches physical location to a locator, and Multicast Info represents a group entry using an instance identifier and source and group prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each approved type describes a different kind of value, such as a private-network identifier, a location, or multicast information. An AFI List can also combine several encoded values.

sections.title: Unapproved Experimental Types
sections.content:
The RFC also documents experimental types that are not in the initial IANA registration. They include Application Data, Opaque Key, Nonce Locator, JSON Data Model, Key/Value Address Pair, and Encapsulation Format.

These encodings are included for further study of their function, demand, and deployment considerations. The RFC restricts them to cautious use in self-contained environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Several documented types are still experimental and are not in the initial registry. The RFC says to use them cautiously in self-contained environments.

sections.title: Privacy and Security
sections.content:
The RFC advises users to consider how the LISP-SEC threat model applies to each use case. Geo-Coordinates can expose sensitive physical locations, including the location of a router in a person's home, so a mapping system should avoid returning location information without a need.

NAT-Traversal and MAC-address encodings also call for policy controls. The RFC recommends that future LISP work consider privacy threats beyond those discussed in RFC 6280.
sections.plainLanguage: Some LCAF values reveal physical locations or network addresses. Operators should apply policies that limit when those values are shared.
